_link.title: I can trace the change in filtrate composition from the Bowman's capsule to the collecting duct

toLevel2.stem: What percentage of the original filtrate remains by the end of the proximal tubule?

explanations.a: Incorrect. 100% of filtrate is present only at Bowman's capsule, before any reabsorption occurs.
explanations.b: Correct. The proximal tubule reabsorbs 65% of water and ions plus 100% of glucose and amino acids, leaving 20% of the original filtrate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. 14% of filtrate remains after the descending loop of Henle, not after the proximal tubule.
explanations.d: Incorrect. 5% of filtrate remains after the distal tubule.

toLevel2.stem: Which substances are present in the filtrate at Bowman's capsule but absent from normal urine?

options.text: Glucose and amino acids
Urea and water
Sodium and chloride ions
Proteins and red blood cells

explanations.a: Correct. Glucose and amino acids are present in the initial filtrate but are fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so they are absent from normal urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Urea and water are present in both the filtrate and urine.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Some sodium and chloride ions remain in urine, though most are reabsorbed.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Proteins and red blood cells are too large to enter the filtrate at Bowman's capsule in the first place.

toLevel2.stem: What is the approximate percentage of the original filtrate that remains as urine at the end of the collecting duct?

explanations.a: Incorrect. 5% of filtrate remains after the distal tubule, not at the end of the collecting duct.
explanations.b: Incorrect. 14% remains after the descending loop of Henle.
explanations.c: Correct. By the end of the collecting duct, 99% of filtrate has been reabsorbed, leaving approximately 1% as urine.
explanations.d: Incorrect. 20% remains after the proximal tubule.

toLevel2.stem: What is the general composition of normal urine?

options.text: 95% water and 5% urea and other substances
50% water and 50% glucose
95% urea and 5% water
80% water and 20% proteins

explanations.a: Correct. Normal urine is approximately 95% water, with urea and other substances making up the remaining 5%.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Glucose is fully reabsorbed and not present in normal urine.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Urine is mostly water, not mostly urea.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Proteins are not present in normal urine as they are too large to be filtered.

toLevel2.stem: In which region of the nephron are 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids reabsorbed?

options.text: The proximal tubule
The distal tubule
The loop of Henle
The collecting duct

explanations.a: Correct. The proximal tubule reabsorbs all filtered glucose and amino acids via active transport.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The distal tubule fine-tunes water and ion balance; glucose has already been reabsorbed.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The loop of Henle reabsorbs water and ions, not glucose or amino acids.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The collecting duct adjusts water content; glucose reabsorption occurs much earlier.

toLevel2.stem: Proteins are present in the filtrate at Bowman's capsule.

distractor.explanation: Proteins are too large to pass through the walls of the glomerular capillaries, so they are not present in the filtrate at Bowman's capsule.

toLevel2.stem: Urea becomes more concentrated as filtrate moves through the nephron because water is reabsorbed while urea largely remains.

distractor.explanation: This statement is true. As water is reabsorbed along the nephron, the concentration of urea increases from about 0.03% in blood plasma to approximately 2% in urine.

toLevel2.stem: The filtrate in Bowman's capsule contains water, glucose, amino acids, ions and {{blank:1}}, but does not contain {{blank:2}}.
After the proximal tubule, {{blank:1}}% of the original filtrate remains because 65% of water and ions have been reabsorbed.
The concentration of urea rises from approximately 0.03% in blood plasma to {{blank:1}}% in urine.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the concentration of urea increase as filtrate moves through the nephron?

options.text: Because water is reabsorbed while urea is largely left behind, so urea becomes more concentrated
Because more urea is added to the filtrate by secretion at every region
Because urea is produced by cells lining the nephron tubule
Because proteins are broken down into urea within the nephron

explanations.a: Correct. As the nephron reabsorbs water, the volume of filtrate decreases but the amount of urea stays relatively constant, so its concentration increases.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While some secretion occurs, the main reason for urea concentration is water removal, not urea addition.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Urea is produced in the liver, not in the nephron tubule.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Proteins do not enter the filtrate and are not broken down within the nephron.

toLevel3.stem: Why is glucose absent from normal urine even though it is present in the filtrate at Bowman's capsule?

options.text: Because the proximal tubule fully reabsorbs glucose using active transport carrier proteins
Because glucose is too large to pass through the collecting duct
Because the loop of Henle breaks glucose down into water and carbon dioxide
Because glucose is converted to urea before reaching the distal tubule

explanations.a: Correct. Specific carrier proteins in the proximal tubule actively transport all filtered glucose back into the blood via the peritubular capillaries.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Glucose is a small molecule that passes easily through tubule walls; its absence is due to reabsorption, not size exclusion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The loop of Henle does not break down glucose. Glucose is reabsorbed earlier in the proximal tubule.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Glucose is not converted to urea in the nephron. Urea is produced from amino acid deamination in the liver.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the filtrate volume drop from 20% to 14% in the descending limb of the loop of Henle?

options.text: Because water moves out of the tubule by osmosis into the surrounding hypertonic medulla
Because ions are actively pumped out, carrying water with them
Because glucose is reabsorbed in the descending limb
Because the descending limb is impermeable to water, so filtrate is compressed

explanations.a: Correct. The descending limb is permeable to water. The surrounding medulla has a high solute concentration, so water leaves by osmosis, reducing filtrate volume from 20% to 14%.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Ion pumping occurs in the ascending limb, not the descending limb.
explanations.c: Incorrect. All glucose has already been reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The descending limb is permeable to water. It is the ascending limb that is impermeable to water.

toLevel3.stem: What happens to the ion concentration of filtrate in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

options.text: Ion concentration decreases because sodium and chloride are actively pumped out while water cannot follow
Ion concentration increases because water is removed by osmosis
Ion concentration stays the same because neither ions nor water can cross the wall
Ion concentration increases because urea is added by secretion

explanations.a: Correct. The ascending limb actively transports Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out of the filtrate. Because the walls are impermeable to water, water stays in the tubule and the filtrate becomes more dilute.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water cannot leave the ascending limb because its walls are impermeable to water.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Ions are actively pumped out of the ascending limb; only water is blocked.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Urea secretion does not occur in the ascending limb.

toLevel3.stem: How does the composition of filtrate change between the distal tubule and the collecting duct?

options.text: Additional water may be reabsorbed under ADH control, further concentrating the urea and reducing volume from 5% to 1%
Glucose is reabsorbed for the first time in the collecting duct
Proteins are added to the filtrate to form urine
All remaining ions are removed, leaving only pure water as urine

explanations.a: Correct. ADH increases the permeability of the distal tubule and collecting duct to water, allowing more water to be reabsorbed by osmosis, concentrating the remaining urea and waste from 5% down to 1%.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Glucose is fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. None remains by the time filtrate reaches the collecting duct.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Proteins are never present in the filtrate and are not added to form urine.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Urine contains ions, urea and other waste products, not just water.

toLevel3.stem: Why is it significant that the filtrate at Bowman's capsule has the same solute composition as blood plasma (minus proteins)?

options.text: It shows that filtration is non-selective, removing all small solutes including useful ones, making reabsorption essential
It shows that the glomerulus selectively removes only waste products
It means no further processing of filtrate is needed
It proves that the kidneys do not process enough blood volume

explanations.a: Correct. Because filtration pushes all small solutes (glucose, amino acids, ions, urea) into the capsule, the nephron must reabsorb useful substances to prevent their loss in urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Filtration is non-selective; both useful and waste solutes enter the filtrate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Without reabsorption, the body would lose glucose, amino acids and water essential for survival.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The kidneys filter about 180 L of plasma daily, which is a very large volume.

toLevel3.stem: After the ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the filtrate has a lower ion concentration than when it entered because ions were pumped out while water was retained.

distractor.explanation: This is true. The ascending limb actively transports Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out while being impermeable to water, so ions leave but water stays, making the filtrate more dilute.

toLevel3.stem: Glucose is absent from normal urine because it is completely reabsorbed in the {{blank:1}} by active transport.
In the descending limb of the loop of Henle, water leaves by {{blank:1}} because the surrounding medulla has a {{blank:2}} solute concentration.
The filtrate volume decreases from 100% at Bowman's capsule to {{blank:1}}% after the proximal tubule and finally to {{blank:2}}% at the collecting duct.

toLevel4.stem: A patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes has very high blood glucose. What would you predict about their urine composition?

options.text: Glucose would be present in urine because the proximal tubule carriers become saturated and cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose
Glucose would still be absent because the collecting duct reabsorbs any excess
Urea would be absent because glucose replaces urea in the filtrate
Protein would appear in urine because high glucose damages the glomerulus immediately

explanations.a: Correct. When blood glucose is abnormally high, more glucose is filtered than the carrier proteins can reabsorb. The excess glucose remains in the filtrate and appears in urine (glycosuria).
explanations.b: Incorrect. The collecting duct does not have glucose transport mechanisms. Glucose reabsorption occurs only in the proximal tubule.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Urea is still present in the filtrate regardless of glucose levels.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While long-term diabetes can damage the glomerulus, the immediate effect of high blood glucose is glucose overflow in urine, not protein leakage.

toLevel4.stem: A researcher collects fluid samples from different parts of the nephron. Sample X contains water, ions and urea but no glucose or amino acids. Where was this sample most likely collected?

options.text: After the proximal tubule
At Bowman's capsule
In the glomerulus
In the renal artery

explanations.a: Correct. By the end of the proximal tubule, 100% of glucose and amino acids have been reabsorbed, but water, ions and urea are still present.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Filtrate at Bowman's capsule still contains glucose and amino acids.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The glomerulus contains blood, including proteins, glucose and amino acids.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The renal artery carries unfiltered blood with all plasma components including proteins.

toLevel4.stem: If a drug inhibits active transport in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle, how would the filtrate composition change?

options.text: Sodium and chloride ions would remain in the filtrate, producing dilute, high-volume urine
Glucose would appear in the urine
Proteins would leak into the filtrate
The filtrate would become more concentrated with ions

explanations.a: Correct. Blocking ion pumping in the ascending limb keeps Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the filtrate. This also reduces the medullary concentration gradient, so less water is reabsorbed in the descending limb and collecting duct, producing more dilute urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Glucose reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule and is unaffected by ascending limb transport.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Protein filtration is determined at the glomerulus, not by transport in the loop of Henle.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Blocking ion removal would prevent concentration of ions outside the tubule; ions would remain in the filtrate, making it more dilute relative to normal.

toLevel4.stem: A fluid sample from the nephron has a volume representing 14% of the original filtrate. At which point in the nephron was it most likely collected?

options.text: End of the descending limb of the loop of Henle
End of the proximal tubule
End of the distal tubule
End of the collecting duct

explanations.a: Correct. The filtrate volume drops from 20% (after proximal tubule) to 14% by the end of the descending loop of Henle due to water reabsorption by osmosis.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The proximal tubule leaves 20% of the original filtrate.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The distal tubule leaves approximately 5% of the original filtrate.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The collecting duct leaves approximately 1% as urine.

toLevel4.stem: A patient's urine test reveals protein. What does this indicate about their nephron function?

options.text: The glomerular capillary walls are damaged, allowing proteins to pass into the filtrate
The proximal tubule is not reabsorbing proteins
The collecting duct is adding proteins to the urine
The loop of Henle is breaking down amino acids into proteins

explanations.a: Correct. Normally, proteins are too large to pass through the glomerular capillary walls. If protein is found in urine, it indicates damage to the filtration barrier.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Proteins should not enter the filtrate in the first place. The proximal tubule does not normally need to reabsorb proteins.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The collecting duct does not produce or add proteins to urine.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Amino acids are small molecules already present in filtrate; the loop of Henle does not synthesise proteins.

toLevel4.stem: If ADH levels are very low, how would the composition of urine change compared to normal?

options.text: Urine would be more dilute and higher in volume because less water is reabsorbed in the distal tubule and collecting duct
Urine would contain glucose because ADH controls glucose reabsorption
Urine would be more concentrated because the collecting duct becomes more permeable
Urine volume would decrease because ADH blocks water reabsorption

explanations.a: Correct. Low ADH means the distal tubule and collecting duct remain less permeable to water. Less water is reabsorbed, so urine is more dilute and volume is higher.
explanations.b: Incorrect. ADH controls water permeability, not glucose reabsorption. Glucose is handled by the proximal tubule.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Low ADH reduces water permeability, producing dilute urine, not concentrated urine.
explanations.d: Incorrect. ADH promotes water reabsorption; low ADH means less reabsorption and more urine, not less.

toLevel4.stem: Two filtrate samples are compared: Sample A from Bowman's capsule and Sample B from the end of the collecting duct. How would their urea concentrations compare?

options.text: Sample B has a much higher urea concentration because water has been removed while urea remained
Both samples have the same urea concentration
Sample A has a higher urea concentration because it is closer to the blood supply
Sample B has no urea because it was all reabsorbed

explanations.a: Correct. As 99% of water is reabsorbed, urea becomes increasingly concentrated. Urea rises from about 0.03% in plasma/initial filtrate to about 2% in final urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The concentration changes dramatically because water removal concentrates the remaining solutes.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sample A reflects plasma concentration (~0.03% urea), which is lower than the concentrated urine.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Urea is a waste product that is largely excreted, not fully reabsorbed.

toLevel4.stem: In uncontrolled diabetes, glucose appears in urine because the {{blank:1}} in the proximal tubule become saturated and cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose.
A filtrate sample containing water, ions and urea but no glucose or amino acids was most likely collected after the {{blank:1}}.
When ADH levels are low, the distal tubule and collecting duct become less permeable to {{blank:1}}, resulting in {{blank:2}} urine volume.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why the filtrate composition changes most dramatically in the proximal tubule compared to other nephron regions.

options.text: The proximal tubule handles bulk reabsorption of 65% of water and ions plus 100% of glucose and amino acids, making it the site of the greatest compositional change
The proximal tubule is the longest region of the nephron, so more time is available for changes
The proximal tubule adds the most waste to the filtrate by secretion
The proximal tubule performs filtration, which is the most significant process

explanations.a: Correct. The proximal tubule removes 80% of the filtrate volume and completely eliminates glucose and amino acids. No other single region removes as much or as many different substances.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While the proximal tubule is a substantial structure, the dramatic change is due to the active transport mechanisms present, not simply its length.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The proximal tubule is primarily a site of reabsorption, not secretion. Secretion occurs mainly at the distal tubule.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Filtration occurs at the glomerulus/Bowman's capsule, not the proximal tubule.

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'The ascending limb does not change the volume of filtrate, so it is not important for urine formation.' Evaluate this claim.

options.text: It is flawed because the ascending limb creates the concentration gradient in the medulla that drives water reabsorption in the descending limb and collecting duct
It is correct because only water reabsorption matters for urine formation
It is correct because the ascending limb is impermeable to both water and ions
It is flawed because the ascending limb reabsorbs large amounts of water

explanations.a: Correct. Although the ascending limb does not directly remove water, it pumps Na⁺ and Cl⁻ into the medulla, creating the high solute concentration that drives osmotic water reabsorption from the descending limb and collecting duct. Without it, the kidney could not concentrate urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Ion composition also matters for urine formation and overall body homeostasis.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively transports ions out of the filtrate.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The ascending limb does not reabsorb water; it is impermeable to water.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the filtrate at the end of the descending limb with the filtrate at the end of the ascending limb. How do they differ?

options.text: The descending limb filtrate has lower volume and higher solute concentration; the ascending limb filtrate has similar volume but lower ion concentration
Both have identical composition because they are parts of the same loop
The ascending limb filtrate contains glucose that was not present in the descending limb
The descending limb filtrate has more ions because water was added

explanations.a: Correct. The descending limb loses water (volume decreases, solutes concentrate). The ascending limb then pumps out ions while retaining water (volume stays similar, but ion concentration drops). This countercurrent mechanism is essential for concentrating urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Though connected, the two limbs have very different permeability properties and the filtrate changes significantly between them.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Glucose was fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule before the loop of Henle.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The descending limb loses water, it does not gain water.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'Finding glucose in urine always means the proximal tubule is damaged.' Is this claim valid?

options.text: No, because glucose can also appear in urine when blood glucose is so high that carrier proteins become saturated, as in uncontrolled diabetes
Yes, because the proximal tubule is the only site of glucose reabsorption and any failure must be structural
No, because glucose is also reabsorbed in the collecting duct
Yes, because blood glucose levels never exceed the capacity of carrier proteins

explanations.a: Correct. Glucose in urine (glycosuria) can occur either from proximal tubule damage or from excess blood glucose saturating the transport carriers, as happens in uncontrolled diabetes. The proximal tubule may be functioning normally but simply overwhelmed.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While the proximal tubule is indeed the only site, the failure is not always structural. Carrier saturation due to high blood glucose is a common cause.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The collecting duct does not reabsorb glucose.
explanations.d: Incorrect. In diabetes, blood glucose can exceed the transport maximum of carrier proteins.

toLevel5.stem: Why does the filtrate change from 5% to 1% of original volume between the distal tubule and collecting duct, but this change is variable rather than fixed?

options.text: Because ADH levels vary with hydration status, making the collecting duct's water permeability adjustable
Because the collecting duct changes length depending on how much urine needs to be produced
Because the proximal tubule adjusts its reabsorption to compensate
Because the glomerular filtration rate changes to match collecting duct capacity

explanations.a: Correct. ADH from the posterior pituitary increases water channel insertion in the collecting duct. When dehydrated, high ADH means more water reabsorption and concentrated urine; when hydrated, low ADH means dilute, high-volume urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The collecting duct does not change its physical length. Water permeability is regulated hormonally.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The proximal tubule performs consistent bulk reabsorption regardless of ADH levels.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While filtration rate can change, the variability in final urine volume is primarily due to ADH's effect on the collecting duct.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why the nephron reabsorbs glucose and amino acids completely but does not reabsorb all urea.

options.text: Glucose and amino acids are essential nutrients with dedicated transport carriers, while urea is a toxic waste product that must be excreted
Urea molecules are too large to be reabsorbed
There are no carrier proteins for urea anywhere in the nephron
Urea is fully reabsorbed but then secreted again in the distal tubule

explanations.a: Correct. The body invests energy in specific carrier proteins to recover valuable glucose and amino acids. Urea is the end product of protein metabolism and is toxic, so the nephron is designed to excrete it rather than recover it.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Urea is a small molecule that can cross membranes. Some passive urea reabsorption does occur, but the nephron does not actively recover it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Some urea is passively reabsorbed along concentration gradients, but there is no active recovery mechanism because urea is waste.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While small amounts of urea are passively reabsorbed and recycled, the net effect is excretion, not complete reabsorption and re-secretion.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether measuring urea concentration alone in a urine sample provides sufficient information to assess kidney function.

options.text: No, because urea concentration depends on both filtration rate and water reabsorption; additional markers like protein presence and urine volume are needed
Yes, because urea concentration directly reflects glomerular filtration rate
Yes, because urea is the only waste product the kidney excretes
No, because urea is not found in urine

explanations.a: Correct. Urea concentration is affected by diet, hydration and both filtration and reabsorption efficiency. A full assessment requires multiple measures including urine volume, presence of protein or glucose, and blood markers.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Urea concentration is influenced by water reabsorption as well as filtration. A dehydrated person may have concentrated urea without any kidney impairment.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The kidney excretes many waste products including excess ions, drugs, and metabolic by-products.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Urea is the major nitrogenous waste product in urine.

toLevel5.stem: A drug blocks water channels in the collecting duct. Trace the effect on filtrate composition and urine output.

options.text: Water cannot be reabsorbed in the collecting duct, so urine volume increases and urea concentration decreases
Glucose appears in urine because water channels also transport glucose
Urine volume decreases because water is trapped in the collecting duct
Ion reabsorption stops because water channels control ion movement

explanations.a: Correct. Without water channels, the collecting duct cannot reabsorb water even with ADH present. More water remains in the tubule, increasing urine volume and diluting urea concentration.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Water channels (aquaporins) transport water only, not glucose. Glucose reabsorption uses different carrier proteins in the proximal tubule.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Blocking water channels prevents water from leaving the tubule, increasing (not decreasing) the volume of urine produced.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Ion transport uses separate channels and pumps, not water channels.

toLevel5.stem: The ascending limb creates the medullary concentration gradient by pumping {{blank:1}} out while being impermeable to {{blank:2}}, enabling water reabsorption in surrounding structures.
Glucose in urine can result from carrier protein {{blank:1}} in the proximal tubule when blood glucose exceeds the transport maximum, as occurs in uncontrolled {{blank:2}}.
